query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor fraction of a self‐lubricating nano‐additive into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix will trigger the in-situ formation of a stable, adaptive lubricious tribofilm during sliding that reduces both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix with its native (likely coarse or partially refined) grain structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor addition of a self‐lubricating nano‐additive directly into the alloy matrix.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted under variable temperatures (from ~25 °C to 800 °C), with moderate-to-high loads and in environments where oxidation effects are present (ambient conditions or controlled atmospheres that mimic service environments).
generation.structural_mediator: The nano-additive is expected to catalyze the formation of a continuous lubricious tribofilm at the sliding interface and possibly promote dynamic grain refinement, thereby modifying the surface microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, the additive activates tribochemically to form an in-situ lubricious film that reduces the shear strength at the contact interface. This film mitigates oxidation damage (as seen in other self-lubricating systems) and maintains a low friction coefficient and wear rate over a broad temperature range, similar to the beneficial effects observed in lubricated HEA systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified alloy will maintain a lower and more stable coefficient of friction and exhibit reduced wear rates across the full operational temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated CoCrFeNi matrix, which under sliding conditions tends to show increased friction and wear—especially at elevated temperatures where oxidation and surface degradation can occur.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is expected to hold within the temperature range of 25 °C to 800 °C under sliding loads typical for tribological testing; deviations in environmental corrosivity or temperatures exceeding this range may affect film stability and performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in friction and wear metrics are uncertain, and interactions between the nano-additive and the alloy matrix under various dynamic conditions require further detailed investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set with the self-lubricating nano-additive uniformly incorporated and a control set without the additive. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests over a temperature gradient from 25 °C to 800 °C under identical load and environmental conditions. Utilize in-situ friction measurements and post-test surface analyses to assess tribofilm formation.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Specific wear rate determined by wear volume measurements
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, TEM) to detect tribofilm formation
Phase analysis of the formed film (e.g., XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nano-additive samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant decrease in both the friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the control samples across the tested temperature range, or if the anticipated lubricious tribofilm is absent, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism
